passages.where: God has brought a case against his people, with the mountains as witnesses. A worshiper asks what offering could satisfy him: calves, rivers of oil, even a firstborn child. The prophet answers that God has already shown what is good, and the chapter goes on to name the false weights and violence of Jerusalem's markets.

Amos speaks to a prosperous kingdom with crowded festivals, while the village court at the city gate, where an ordinary person could find a fair hearing, has been bought. God says he hates their feasts. He does not ask for less worship; he asks for justice to flow like a river that does not run dry.

The people are fasting and asking why God does not notice. God answers that on their fast days they exploit their workers and quarrel. The fast he chooses is to loosen the chains of injustice, feed the hungry, take in the homeless and clothe the naked, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood.

In the chapter that calls Israel to be holy as God is holy, the first concrete command is about the harvest. A farmer was not to strip his field to the edges or go back for what fell, so that the poor and the foreigner could gather it with their own hands. Provision for the poor was built into ordinary work.

The same chapter forbids bending justice in either direction: no partiality to the poor and no favoritism to the rich. Biblical justice is not taking a side by class. It is judging a neighbor fairly, which in a world tilted toward the powerful usually means defending the weak.

Every seventh year Israelite creditors were to cancel the debts of their own people. Moses warns against refusing a loan because the year of release is near. The fact that there will always be poor people in the land is given as the reason to open the hand wide, not to close it.

Jeremiah confronts King Jehoiakim, who built himself a lavish palace with labor he did not pay for. He sets him beside his father Josiah, who defended the cause of the poor and needy, and then asks the question that makes this passage remarkable: is this not what it means to know the LORD?

King Lemuel records what his mother taught him: do not waste your strength or dull your judgment with wine, because a king's work is to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves. Power is given for the sake of those who have none.

In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads from Isaiah about the one anointed to bring good news to the poor and release to the oppressed, and says it is fulfilled today. In Luke's account this is his own statement of his mission, and each line comes true somewhere in the Gospel.

A rich man feasts every day, and a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate, covered in sores and hungry for the crumbs. The parable says nothing of what the rich man does at the gate, and that is the point: he passed him every day. After death their places are reversed.

James has just rebuked a church for honoring rich visitors and humiliating poor ones. Now he imagines a believer telling a hungry, cold brother or sister to go in peace and keep warm, and doing nothing. Faith that speaks kindly and does nothing, he says, is dead.

misread.taken: Jesus' words “The poor you will always have with you” are quoted to suggest that poverty is permanent, so efforts to relieve it are naive, or at least not the church's business.
misread.says: Jesus is defending a woman who has poured costly perfume on him shortly before his death, while the disciples complain it could have been sold for the poor. His answer is about timing: this moment, before his burial, calls for this act. His words echo Deuteronomy 15:11, where the continuing presence of the poor is the reason God commands his people to open their hands wide. Read in its place, the saying assumes the disciples will keep giving to the poor long after he is gone.

misread.taken: The scene of the sheep and the goats is read in two opposite ways: as teaching that anyone who helps the poor is saved whatever they believe, or as narrowed so far that it asks nothing of anyone toward the poor around them.
misread.says: Interpreters differ on who “the least of these brothers of Mine” are. One reading, held by many scholars, takes them to be Jesus' disciples, often poor and persecuted, so the nations are judged by how they received his messengers. Another, widely held across Catholic, Protestant and Orthodox teaching, takes them to be all the needy. Neither reading turns the passage into salvation by good deeds apart from Christ, and neither excuses indifference: elsewhere the New Testament tells believers to do good to everyone, especially to the family of faith (Galatians 6:10).

whole: Most people meet this subject sideways. A man with a cardboard sign at the intersection, a neighbor whose hours were cut, a news story about wages or rents, a church budget meeting. It is easy to feel both guilty and helpless, and easy to let the subject become a political argument, where it can be held at a distance and used against someone else. Many Christians have heard sermons that made concern for the poor sound like a distraction from the gospel, and others have heard sermons that made it sound like the whole of it.

Scripture will not let the subject stay at a distance. Its concern for the poor is not a theme in one corner of the Bible. It is in the harvest laws of Leviticus, the debt release of Deuteronomy, the sayings of Proverbs, the thunder of Amos and Isaiah, the mother's counsel to King Lemuel, Jesus' sermon at Nazareth, the parable of the beggar at the gate, and the letter of James. The prophets do not condemn worship; they condemn worship that goes on beside cheated workers and bought courts. Jeremiah goes further and says that defending the cause of the poor is what it means to know God. Justice, in the Bible's sense, is not a program of one party. It is doing right by each person as God's creature, judging fairly without favoritism to rich or poor, and refusing to let the weak be crushed.

The deepest root of this is in God himself. Proverbs says that whoever oppresses the poor insults their Maker, because rich and poor share one Maker. The law kept reminding Israel that they had been slaves and strangers. The church learned the same thing at the cross: everyone who receives grace received it while poor before God, and the Lord who brought it became poor for our sake. That memory is meant to make generosity ordinary, and to make contempt for the poor impossible.

So the wisdom here begins close to home. Notice the person at your own gate, in your own church, at your own work, and do something real; James has no patience for kind words alone. Give, and give with thought. Pay people fairly and on time. Speak for those who cannot speak, as Lemuel's mother asked, wherever you have a voice. Christians will disagree about which public policies serve the poor best, and those disagreements are real. What they may not do is let the argument become a way of doing nothing, or a way of looking down on the people the Bible keeps putting at the center.

differ.share: Christians agree that God cares for the poor and the oppressed, that every person bears his image, that his people are commanded to be generous and to deal justly, and that justice means fair judgment without favoritism to rich or poor.

views.name: Charity, church and neighbor first
views.body: Many Christians hold that the Bible's commands about the poor fall first on persons, families and churches, and are best answered by direct generosity, voluntary associations and the local church. They are wary of looking to government for what neighbors are called to give, and value work, family and local community as the surest paths out of poverty.

views.name: Just laws and public provision
views.body: Many other Christians hold that the Bible's laws on gleaning, debt and wages show that care for the poor was built into Israel's public order, and that the prophets held kings to account for it. They hold that just laws and public provision are among the ways a society answers these commands, alongside personal generosity.

differ.after: Both read the same prophets and both are called to give and act, not only to argue. A Christian on either side should be able to state the other's case in words its holders would sign, and to find the poor in their own neighborhood this week.

sit: Who is lying at your gate, someone you pass so often you no longer see them, and what would one real act toward them look like?

prayer.lead: A prayer for the king, asking God to give him justice for the afflicted and the needy. Pray it for anyone who holds power, and for yourself where you hold some.
